d.title: Distance, then a vote — and every step is a choice
d.caption: There is no training step, so every decision lives at query time. That is what makes KNN a useful baseline in an afternoon and an awkward model in production: the whole training set is the model, and each query scans it.

items.label: Scale the features
items.desc: without this, the distance is a model of the widest column

items.label: Choose a metric
items.desc: Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine — it defines what 'similar' means

items.label: Find the k nearest
items.desc: a scan, or a tree index that stops helping in high dimension

items.label: Vote, or average
items.desc: classification by majority, regression by mean

items.label: Weight by distance
items.desc: closer neighbours count more; smooths the boundary

items.label: Note what k does
items.desc: small k is high variance, large k is high bias: the dial of 1.3

d.title: k = 1 has perfect memory and coin-flip generalisation
d.caption: At k = 1 the training AUC is **1.0000** — every query is its own nearest neighbour — while cross-validated AUC is 0.5747, barely better than a coin. That single row is the bias–variance dial of 1.3 made concrete. As k rises the train score falls and the CV score climbs, and the log-loss falls fastest of all because averaging more neighbours stops the model asserting 0 and 1. Scaling first is worth more than any k: unscaled 0.6632 against standardised 0.6914, because the sds are 17.5 for tenure and 0.9 for tickets.

d.title: On the churn data KNN matched logistic regression and cost 400x more per query
d.caption: 0.754 at k = 401 against logistic regression's 0.757 — statistically the same answer. But k = 401 means the model needed almost half the training set as neighbours to be stable, which is a signal that the truth here is near-linear and smooth, and every query pays a scan to rediscover it.

columns.title: Reach for KNN when
items: The boundary is local and curved
A quick assumption-free baseline is wanted
New rows must count with no retraining
You need a similarity lookup or an anomaly score

columns.title: Do not when
items: There is a latency budget: every query scans
Imbalance, with no weighting or threshold work

d.title: From Bayes' theorem to a classifier in three moves
d.caption: The first two steps are exact. The third is the 'naive' one, and it is false in almost every real dataset — features are correlated. What makes the method work anyway is that classification is an **argmax**: the posterior can be wrong in value and still largest for the right class.

nodes.label: Drop the denominator
nodes.sub: it is the same for every class

d.title: Pick the variant from the feature type, not by trial
d.caption: Each variant is a different choice of P(x | y), so the feature type decides it outright. The Bernoulli row is the instructive one: modelling presence rather than counts throws the repetition signal away, which is why it scored 0.836 on the newsgroups where multinomial counts do better.

d.title: Duplicating one column, to watch the naive assumption break
d.caption: The tickets column is copied 1, 4 and 9 times — adding no information whatsoever, and forcing the model to count the same evidence repeatedly. The **ranking barely moves**: AUC drifts 0.735 to 0.686. The calibration is destroyed: log-loss triples, the share of near-certain predictions goes from 40% to 89%, and the top quintile is predicted at 86% churn against an actual 26%. That is the precise cost of the assumption — it corrupts the probabilities, not the ordering.

d.title: The margin, and the problem that maximises it
d.caption: Fix the scale by requiring the closest points to sit at ±1 and the margin becomes 2/‖w‖ — so maximising the margin is **minimising the norm**, a convex quadratic programme with one global solution. The points that end up on the boundary are the support vectors, and they are the only rows the solution depends on: delete every other row and the fit is unchanged.

nodes.label: Minimise ||w||²
nodes.sub: a convex QP: one global answer

nodes.label: Every other row is irrelevant
nodes.sub: delete them; the fit is identical

d.title: The cheapest solution was to give up, and the arithmetic says so
d.caption: Linear SVM, standardised, C = 1, 15.4% positives: the fitted model is **w = (0,0,0,0,0), b = −1** — it predicts 'no churn' for everyone and its decision function is constant, so the 0.629 AUC is noise. Separating 133 scattered positives would need a large norm; abandoning them costs 133 × 2 = 266 of slack, and at C = 1 that is cheaper. Logistic regression never does this, because log-loss keeps pulling on every point while the hinge stops pulling once a point is written off.

items.label: 133 positives, scattered
items.desc: 15.4% of 866 rows, no clean separating direction

items.label: Separating them needs a large norm
items.desc: which the regularisation term charges for

items.label: At C = 1 the slack is cheaper
items.desc: so w = 0 is the optimum: a constant predictor

items.label: AUC 0.629 — and it is noise
items.desc: a constant decision function has no ranking

items.label: class_weight='balanced'
items.desc: minority slack costs 5.5x more; AUC 0.757, every C from 0.001 to 10

d.title: The kernel trick: never build the features
d.caption: The dual solution touches the data only through inner products, so replacing every xᵢ'xⱼ with K(xᵢ, xⱼ) fits a linear model in a **feature space that is never constructed** — for the RBF kernel, one of infinite dimension. The cost is that the solution is now expressed through the training rows rather than a weight vector, so prediction needs the support vectors and scales with n rather than with p.

nodes.label: Replace x'x with K(x, x')
nodes.sub: a kernel: a valid inner product

d.title: SVM and logistic regression, honestly compared
d.caption: The hinge is zero beyond the margin and the log-loss never is — nearly every row below follows from that one difference, including which rows the solution depends on and how each model behaves under imbalance.

d.title: Two candidate splits on six rows, scored three ways
d.caption: Parent: 3 Yes / 3 No, so entropy is 1.000 bit and Gini 0.500. **Wind** sends four rows one way (3Y/1N) and two the other (pure), giving a weighted child entropy of 0.541 and an information gain of 0.459. **Outlook** splits into 1Y/2N and 2Y/1N — both still mixed — for a gain of only 0.082. Every criterion agrees here, and the last column shows why C4.5 added gain ratio: dividing by the split's own entropy penalises a feature for simply having more branches.

d.title: What a depth-3 tree actually learned, and what it is worth
d.caption: A readable model: three levels, eight leaves, and a rule you can print on a card. It scores 0.679 against the forest's 0.724 — so the tree costs about 0.045 of AUC and buys an explanation an on-call engineer can read at three in the morning. The catch from §03 is that the **rules themselves move** between resamples, so the explanation is less stable than it looks.

d.title: Two noise columns ranked with the best real feature
d.caption: A random integer id with 989 distinct values and a random normal, added to the churn features. Mean-decrease-in-impurity ranks the noise at the top: a column with many distinct values offers many candidate thresholds, and among many random thresholds one always looks good on the training rows. Permutation importance puts random_normal at 0.032, and the CV AUC was 0.674 with the noise columns against 0.662 without — the tree used them to memorise.
cells: ranked last here, first by permutation

d.title: Weaker trees, a better forest — and the correlation column explains it
d.caption: The variance of an average falls with the members' **correlation**, not with their individual quality. Reading down: as `max_features` shrinks, each tree gets worse (0.691 to 0.592) and the trees get far less alike (correlation 0.361 to 0.081, sharing 100% of features down to 6%) — and the ensemble holds steady or improves. That is the entire argument for random feature subsets: a committee of mediocre, genuinely different opinions beats a committee of excellent identical ones.

d.title: What each forest dial actually moved
d.caption: Averaging reduces the variance of the mean by a factor that depends on how **correlated** the members are, which is why `max_features` matters: fewer candidates per split makes each tree weaker and the trees less alike, and the second effect wins. The measurements are from the churn data.
cells: no: as large as time allows
yes, a few values near the default

d.title: What a forest fixes, and four things it does not
d.caption: It fixes variance and nothing else. On XOR, depth-2 trees went 0.710 to 0.908 because different bootstraps find different roots and the average recovers the interaction. But an average of staircases is a smoother staircase, still axis-aligned — 0.981 against logistic regression's 0.993 on a diagonal boundary — and every tree is flat beyond its last split, so their mean is too.
cells: every tree is flat past its last split

d.title: AdaBoost on ten points: three stumps, zero errors
d.caption: Each round refits on **reweighted** rows, so the next stump is forced to attend to what the last one got wrong. Watch the weights: round 1 is wrong on x = 6, 7, 8, so their weight rises from 0.1 to 0.167 and the next stump cuts at 8.5 instead. Three stumps — each individually unable to separate the data — sum to an ensemble with zero training errors. Note α grows as the error falls: at ε = 0.5 a learner's vote is zero, and above 0.5 it is negative, which simply means invert it.

d.title: Gradient boosting is gradient descent, with trees as the step
d.caption: The insight that makes the name literal: instead of taking a step in parameter space, take a step in **function** space — and the step direction is the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions, which for squared error is just the residual.

items.label: Start from a constant
items.desc: the mean for squared error, the log-odds for log-loss

items.label: Compute the negative gradient
items.desc: for squared error this is exactly the residual

items.label: Fit a shallow tree to it
items.desc: the tree approximates the descent direction

items.label: Take a small step
items.desc: F = F + nu x h; the learning rate is the step size

items.label: Repeat
items.desc: each tree corrects what the sum so far still gets wrong

items.label: Stop before it fits the noise
items.desc: early stopping is the regulariser; more trees eventually hurt

d.title: Bagging and boosting are opposite machines
d.caption: Bagging reduces variance and leaves bias alone, so more trees never hurt. Boosting reduces bias by construction, so more trees eventually overfit — 0.719 down to 0.596 at a learning rate of 1. That single asymmetry explains the tuning burden: a forest's defaults are safe and a booster's can be the worst model in the room.

d.title: The second-order objective, and the split gain it implies
d.caption: Take a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss around the current prediction and the optimal leaf value falls out in closed form: −G/(H+λ), where G and H are the summed first and second derivatives in that leaf. The gain of a split is then an arithmetic comparison of three such terms — which is why XGBoost can evaluate thousands of candidate splits per node without ever refitting anything.

nodes.label: 2nd-order Taylor of the loss
nodes.sub: gradients g, hessians h per row

nodes.label: lambda and gamma are regularisers
nodes.sub: they appear in the gain itself

d.title: Four libraries, measured on 200k x 30 for 300 rounds
d.caption: They implement the same objective and differ in how a tree is grown and how categoricals are handled. CatBoost's symmetric trees fit slowest and **predict fastest by an order of magnitude** — 0.02 s against 0.38 s — which is the trade to know when latency is the constraint.

d.title: Categoricals without leakage
d.caption: A booster that handles categoricals natively is not thereby safe: naive target statistics computed over all rows leak the label exactly as a hand-rolled target encoder would. CatBoost's ordered boosting is the one that is safe by construction, because each row's statistic uses only rows before it in a permutation.
cells: no, but <= a few hundred levels

d.title: Condorcet's theorem, and the independence that carries all of it
d.caption: Eleven independent voters at 0.60 each give a majority accuracy of **0.750** against the theorem's 0.753, and a hundred and one give 0.979. Make them mildly correlated and eleven fall to 0.630; make them near-copies and 0.606 — eleven copies of one opinion is one opinion. The last row is the warning: with voters **worse** than chance the majority is worse than any member, and more of them is worse still (0.367 at eleven, 0.156 at a hundred and one), because the theorem runs in reverse below 0.5.

d.title: The stacking leak: the meta-model trusted the biggest overfitter
d.caption: Fit three base models, take their predictions **on their own training rows** as meta-features, and the meta-model's coefficients come out [0.97, 2.46, 4.61] — trusting boosting most and logistic regression least, in exactly the order of their *training* AUCs. That is the order of how much they overfit. Out-of-fold meta-features reverse it, because they are the only ones that show how a member behaves on data it has not seen.

d.title: Check the members' correlation before combining anything
d.caption: Above about 0.9 with one clearly best member, the combination lands at or below that member — the churn case, six ways, where the stack predicted 35× slower for −0.005 AUC. Below about 0.8 among comparably good members, averaging gains. The usual outcome on a well-specified problem is that the ensemble's gain is smaller than the gain from a better feature.

cells.text: at or below the best member
